groups.context: A cruel lion ate many forest animals daily until they proposed a deal: one animal would come to him each day, so he wouldn't need to hunt. When it was the rabbit's turn, it arrived late, claiming to have been hiding from 'another lion' who called himself king. Enraged, the lion demanded to be shown this rival — the rabbit led him to a deep well, where the lion saw his own reflection, mistook it for the rival, and leapt in to attack it, never to return. The other animals were delighted by the rabbit's clever trick.

groups.context: Pakistan enjoys four seasons, each with its own gifts. Spring, the 'king of all seasons,' runs late February to May, bringing new leaves and blossoms. Summer (June–August) is long and hot on the plains, milder in hilly areas, with long days and short nights. groups.context: Primitive human beings who were hunter-gatherers had no money. Each band hunted, gathered and manufactured almost everything it required, sharing goods and services through an economy of favors and obligations, occasionally supplemented by simple barter. Little of this changed with the Agricultural Revolution — most people still lived in small, self-sufficient villages. The rise of cities and kingdoms, along with improved transport, finally brought full-time specialization: professional shoemakers, doctors, carpenters, priests, soldiers and lawyers, trading goods between settlements suited to different climates and skills.

groups.context: Syed Ahmed went to England on a dual mission — to learn and to teach. His learning mission succeeded in a year and five months, giving him insight into what made the British rulers of a vast empire. His teaching mission failed: the British had no interest in learning about Islam, being preoccupied instead with science, social reform, and individual liberty. groups.context: Everyone once believed Earth was at the centre of the universe. Copernicus realized this didn't match astronomical observations, and worked out that the Sun was at the centre, with Earth orbiting it once a year while rotating every 24 hours. He believed planetary orbits were perfect circles — fifty years later, Kepler used Tycho Brahe's precise measurements to show they are not.

groups.context: Empires generate huge amounts of information — laws, tax accounts, military inventories, calendars of festivals. For millions of years, humans stored information only in their brains, which is a poor fit for empire-sized databases for three reasons: limited capacity even for trained memory experts; the information dies with the person, degrading further each time it's passed on; and the brain evolved to store botanical, zoological, and social information rather than numbers, since hunter-gatherers never needed to track large numerical data.
